title: Professor Helen X. H. Bao
notes:
Moodle version of Week 5, built on 2026-10-26 from the Week 1 Moodle deck as the format template, in the way Weeks 2, 3, 4 and 7 were built. 20 slides against the 30 asked for. The earlier 68-slide deck is kept beside it (RE07 Week 5 - Intermediation and Deal Brokerage.pptx) as the source of material; it is untouched and describes the earlier shape of the week, organised in blocks around why intermediaries exist, who they are, arranging and syndication, fees, and whether they add value.

SHAPE OF THE DECK

The first hour is broad and the second hour zooms in. The survey (slides 3 to 9) has three parts, each anchored in a paper, a textbook chapter or a report whose pages I read: arranging and certifying a financing (3 slides on the fee stack, the structures of syndication and the evidence on arranger prestige), brokerage, advice and manager selection (3 slides: the sale of a house with and without an agent, the effect of the 2024 settlement on agents' fees, and investment consultants) and private credit in the data-centre boom (1 slide). The focus part (slides 10 to 18) takes one question, what an intermediary is paid for and what keeps it honest, through three models with an interactive page each: Duffie, Gârleanu and Pedersen (2005) on immediacy, Berk and Green (2004) on skill, and Franzoni (1999) on assurance. The pages open on generic settings. Then the case (1 slide, headings only) and the summary. There is no thank-you slide.

NO CASE IS CONFIRMED FOR THIS WEEK

The week's guest, Justin Chiu, has agreed to serve on the Panel and to take the case hour, but no topic is agreed. The first hour is therefore broad, and the three focus models are general: each is something a real transaction, whichever it is, can test. The case slide lists kinds of evidence, not a case.

DATA CENTRES

The week's aspect of the course thread on data centres is who stands between the hyperscaler and the money: private credit funds, which originate and hold, in slide 9, set against the older originate-to-distribute banks of slide 4. Week 4 slides 4 and 5 gave the Hyperion structure; this week asks who arranged it, who bought it and what each was paid, which the sources I could read do not answer, and the case slide records that as a question for the guest.

PAGE NUMBERS AND WHAT IS NOT VERIFIED

Every source is cited in the notes of its slide with page numbers, which are the printed page numbers of the version I read, and each note states the offset. Several are working papers: Gatti, Kleimeier, Megginson and Steffanoni is the draft of 19 March 2007, whose published version is Financial Management 42(1), 2013 (I could not retrieve it, so check the final wording before quoting); Hendel, Nevo and Ortalo-Magné is NBER Working Paper 13360 of September 2007, published in the American Economic Review 99(5), 2009; Jenkinson, Jones and Martinez is the September 2014 draft, published in the Journal of Finance (I recall volume 71, 2016); Berk and van Binsbergen is NBER Working Paper 18184 of June 2012, published in the Journal of Financial Economics (I recall 2015); Buchak and others is the October 2025 revision of NBER Working Paper 32855; Grochulski and Wang is the December 2025 revision of Richmond Fed Working Paper 24-01. Sufi (2007) and Golubov, Petmezas and Travlos (2012), which the earlier deck used, I could read only at the level of abstract and could not retrieve, so Sufi is mentioned in one line with that caveat and Golubov is left out. Two models I would have liked, Bolton, Freixas and Shapiro (2012) on rating agencies and Lizzeri (1999) on certification, could not be retrieved, and Franzoni (1999), a Bologna working paper that I could read in full, stands in for them. The printed formulas for the fee in the Franzoni equilibrium are hard to read in my copy; I derived the equilibrium and checked it by brute force, and its limits agree with the paper's own, but the paper should be checked.

WHAT WAS CUT FROM THE EARLIER DECK

The fee stack, the structures of syndication and the evidence that arrangers certify (old slides 24 to 40) are compressed into slides 3 to 5, with the worked example from Gatti's tables. The three tests of whether intermediaries add value (old 41 to 49) are compressed into slides 6 to 8 and the focus part, with Golubov and the Demirag interviews dropped because I could not check them. The four frictions (old 5 and 6) became the three things an intermediary can sell (slide 10). The fund management fee slide (old 36) is covered by the Week 1 fee page and by slide 13. The guest block for a single principal (old block G) is replaced by the case slide and the notes below it.

Spoken: 'The first hour is a map of how a financing is assembled, who is paid for what, and what we know about whether they add value, from loans to houses to fund managers. The middle of the hour is three models of what an intermediary sells, each with a page you can run. Then you meet one principal and we ask what it says about the models.'

title: The Fee Stack on a Syndicated Loan
notes:
THE FIGURE

Gatti (2024), Project Finance in Theory and Practice, Tables 6.8 to 6.10, printed pages 207 and 208 (PDF page less 19). A syndicated project loan of EUR 200 million. The sponsor pays an adviser (Bank A) a success fee of 0.75 per cent, EUR 1.5 million, and a mandated lead arranger (Bank B) an arranging fee of 1 per cent, EUR 2.0 million. Bank B underwrites EUR 100 million with the co-arranger Bank C and passes on parts of the fee: co-arranging fees of 0.80 per cent to each of the two underwriters and up-front management fees of 0.20 per cent to the managers. The left panel shows what each bank keeps of the EUR 2.0 million (0.85, 0.85, 0.08, 0.10 and 0.12, which add to 2.00). The right panel shows each fee as a return on the capital the bank finally lends (EUR 25 million each for Banks B and C and EUR 40, 50 and 60 million for the managers): 3.40 per cent for the two lead banks and 0.20 per cent for the managers (Table 6.10).

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The sponsor pays EUR 3.5 million, 1.75 per cent of the loan, before the first drawdown. Market standards for the fees are in the text: advisory success fees of 0.5 to 1 per cent of the debt, arranging fees of 0.7 to 1 per cent of the syndicated debt, up-front management fees of 20 to 40 basis points on each lender's amount, and co-arrangers paid 0.5 to 0.8 per cent of the part they underwrite (pages 204 to 205). The fee is on the debt and not on the project cost, and the author gives two reasons: a sponsor would not pay a fee on its own equity, and a fee linked to the loan gives the adviser an incentive to plan the highest possible debt (page 205). That second reason is the one to put to the class: the adviser's fee rises with the leverage it recommends. The unequal split is the author's point that the lead arranger's strong position lets it return less to the others: if the others won the whole 1 per cent, which is the club deal, the lead arranger would earn the same as the co-arranger (page 208).

CAUTIONS

The amounts are illustrative, for a loan of EUR 200 million, and are not market data. The percentages in the text are market standards as the author states them, without a date or a source in the passage I read. The return on capital treats the whole fee as a return on the part each bank lends, and ignores the cost of underwriting risk during the syndication, which is what the fee partly pays for. A retainer fee for the adviser (EUR 15,000 to 25,000 a month on the author's figures, page 204) and an agent's annual fee are left out.

SOURCE

Gatti, S. (2024), Project Finance in Theory and Practice, third edition, Academic Press, chapter 6, pages 204 to 208; Tables 6.8 and 6.9 (page 207) and 6.10 (page 208).

A CASE COULD SUPPLY

The fees actually paid on a financing the guest knows: advisory, arranging and underwriting fees, the split among banks, and whether the adviser and the arranger were the same institution.
text: The Fee Stack on a Syndicated Loan 4 What the sponsor pays: EUR 1.5 million to the adviser and EUR 2.0 million to the arranger on a loan of EUR 200 million, 1.75 per cent before the first drawdown Who keeps it: the two lead banks keep EUR 0.85 million each and the three managers EUR 0.08 to 0.12 million The return on capital: 3.4 per cent on the EUR 25 million each lead bank finally lends, 0.2 per cent for managers who lend EUR 40 to 60 million The incentive: the adviser's fee is a share of the debt, so it rises with the leverage the adviser recommends Gatti (2024), Project Finance in Theory and Practice, Tables 6.8 to 6.10, printed pages 207 and 208. Illustrative loan of EUR 200 million; Banks B and C lend EUR 25 million each, Banks D, E and F lend EUR 40, 50 and 60 million.

title: Underwriting, Club Deals and the Debt Fund
notes:
THE TABLE

Five ways in which a large infrastructure loan has been assembled, from Gatti (2024), sections 6.2.1 and 6.2.2, printed pages 191 to 196 (PDF page less 19).

Two-stage syndication: a mandated arranger gathers a small group of underwriters and then resells part of the loan in a general syndication. The final take the arranger keeps is usually around 10 per cent of the loan, and the author explains the trade-off: a smaller final take lowers risk and raises the return on capital, but selling too much signals that the arranger lacks confidence and weakens its incentive to monitor (page 192). Before the financial crisis the whole process took one or two months, sometimes up to twelve for very large projects (page 192).

Club deals: a restricted pool of banks, normally four to six, jointly proposes the whole financing with a full commitment, so the first stage of the syndication becomes the only stage. They are quicker and shield the banks from changes in market conditions, but all the banks have the same role and the fees are shared equally, so the lead arranger cannot earn more than the others (page 193).

Partnership with an institutional investor: an institution invests in loans a bank originates and participates in a standard syndication, relying on the bank's screening and monitoring, and the bank keeps a pre-agreed share. The text gives Crédit Agricole, which transferred EUR 1 billion of loans to its insurance arm in the first half of 2012 and kept 20 per cent (page 195). The author adds that after 2018 many banks dropped the model in favour of co-investing with several institutions (page 195).

Securitisation: loans pooled and sold as rated notes. The market for securitisations of infrastructure loans, project finance CLOs and CDOs, 'has almost disappeared' since 2008, and the resurgence of the originate-to-distribute model has revived interest in it (pages 195 to 196).

Debt fund: an institution commits to a fund managed by an asset manager. From 2010 to 2020, 170 infrastructure debt funds reached a financial close and raised roughly USD 88 billion, 12 per cent of the capital committed by investors, from USD 1 billion in 2010 (page 196).

THE POINT

The same function, finding a lender who will hold a loan for a long time, is performed by a bank syndicate, by an institution co-investing alongside a bank and by a fund, and the fee that goes with it differs with whose balance sheet bears the risk and for how long. The slide is the bridge to the data-centre slide that follows, in which private credit funds originate and hold the loan themselves.

CAUTIONS

The figures for the debt funds are the author's, from a source he cites but I did not read, and are those of a stated period and not a current count. The fee comments are qualitative: the textbook does not give a fee for the debt fund model.

SOURCE

Gatti, S. (2024), Project Finance in Theory and Practice, third edition, sections 6.2.1 and 6.2.2, printed pages 191 to 196.

A CASE COULD SUPPLY

Which of the five structures a financing used, who held the loan at year five and at year ten, and how the arranger's final take was chosen.
text: Underwriting, Club Deals and the Debt Fund 4 Gatti (2024), Project Finance in Theory and Practice, sections 6.2.1 and 6.2.2, printed pages 191 to 196. Debt fund figures are for 2010 to 2020. Structure How it works What the text records (printed page) Two-stage syndication A small group underwrites, then resells part of the loan; the arranger keeps a final take of around 10 per cent One to two months, up to twelve for very large deals (192) Club deal Four to six banks provide the whole loan; fees are shared equally Quicker, and shields the banks from changes in the market (193) Partnership with an institution An insurer co-invests in loans a bank originates; the bank keeps a share Crédit Agricole kept 20 per cent of EUR 1 billion transferred in 2012 (195) Securitisation Loans pooled and sold as rated notes Project loan CLOs and CDOs almost disappeared after 2008 (195 to 196) Debt fund An institution commits to a fund that originates the loans 170 funds reached close from 2010 to 2020, raising about USD 88 billion (196)

title: Arranger Prestige and Loan Terms
notes:
THE FIGURE

Gatti, Kleimeier, Megginson and Steffanoni, Arranger Certification in Project Finance, draft of 19 March 2007, Table 3 Panel A, printed page 21 (PDF page less one). The loans of the sample are sorted into four groups by the lead arranger's average market share over the previous three years. The mean spread is 193.91, 177.30, 148.72 and 156.12 basis points; the mean up-front fee is 70.17, 74.32, 67.57 and 65.55 basis points; the mean loan size is USD 97.96, 122.26, 160.10 and 186.55 million in real terms (the average leverage, debt to equity, is 3.59, 3.26, 2.76 and 4.08 on 45 to 48 observations, which the authors caution against reading too strongly, page 9 to 10).

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The sample is 4,122 project finance loans worth USD 584 billion arranged from 1991 to 2005 (abstract). The authors test three ideas. Valuable certification: loans with prestigious arrangers should cost less. Direct compensation: prestigious arrangers should earn higher fees. Indirect compensation: prestigious arrangers should be able to place larger and more leveraged loans. The abstract reports that certification creates economic value by reducing overall loan spreads, that top-tier arrangers are not compensated with higher fees but with larger market shares, which rejects direct compensation and supports indirect compensation. The table shows the pattern in the raw data: spreads fall from 194 to 156 basis points, fees do not rise, and loans grow from USD 98 million to USD 187 million. Regressions that control for project risk, in Table 4, are the paper's main evidence, and the text says the spread effect is robust to selection of loans (pages 9 to 10).

The last line on the slide is Sufi (2007), Journal of Finance 62(2), 629 to 668, which I could read only at the level of its abstract (via the RePEc listing): the lead bank keeps a larger share of the loan and forms a more concentrated syndicate when the borrower needs more intensive monitoring and due diligence, which fits moral hazard in monitoring, and participants who face more asymmetric information are closer to the borrower. Gatti's textbook says the same thing as practice: a larger final take is a show of confidence and motivates the arranger to monitor (page 192 of the textbook). The earlier deck gave sample sizes for Sufi that I could not verify and which are left out.

CAUTIONS

The draft is not the published version (Financial Management 42(1), 2013, which I could not retrieve), and the earlier deck's account of who pays for certification, that participants concede a larger share of the fees, is not what the abstract of the draft says, so check the published wording before repeating it. The quartiles use the arranger's market share as a proxy for prestige, and a proxy can be managed by the party it measures: volume is not quality. The table does not control for project risk; the regressions do. The fourth-quartile spread (156) is above the third (149), so do not describe the fall in spread as steady across the four groups.

SOURCE

Gatti, S., Kleimeier, S., Megginson, W. L. and Steffanoni, A. (2007), Arranger Certification in Project Finance, draft of 19 March 2007, abstract and Table 3 (page 21). Published as Financial Management 42(1), 2013 (not retrieved). Sufi, A. (2007), Journal of Finance 62(2), 629 to 668, abstract only.

A CASE COULD SUPPLY

The identity and rank of the arranger on a financing, what it kept, and what the sponsor says it paid for: certification, capacity or access.
text: Arranger Prestige and Loan Terms 4 The sample: 4,122 project finance loans worth USD 584 billion, arranged from 1991 to 2005 Spread: 194 basis points where the lead arranger's market share is lowest, 156 where it is highest Fee: no higher for the larger arrangers: 70 and 66 basis points, so prestige is not paid for directly Size: larger loans, USD 98 million against 187 million: the arranger's name buys capacity Retained share: Sufi (2007): the lead bank keeps more of a loan that needs more monitoring Gatti, Kleimeier, Megginson and Steffanoni (draft of 19 March 2007), Table 3 Panel A, page 21; abstract. Sufi (2007), Journal of Finance 62(2), abstract.

title: Selling a House without an Agent
notes:
THE FIGURE

Hendel, Nevo and Ortalo-Magné, The Relative Performance of Real Estate Marketing Platforms: MLS versus FSBOMadison.com, NBER Working Paper 13360, September 2007, Table 1, printed page 29 (PDF page less one). Madison, Wisconsin, listings from 1998 to 2004, by the platform on which the property was first listed. Of 12,468 listings with an agent on the Multiple Listing Service, 10,725 (86.0 per cent) sold through the MLS, 30 (0.2) sold by the owner and 1,713 (13.7) did not sell. Of 3,138 listings by the owner on the website, 697 (22.2) ended with an agent on the MLS, 2,153 (68.6) sold by the owner and 288 (9.2) did not sell.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The paper compares a new for-sale-by-owner website, which had about a fifth of listings (page 12), rising from 6 per cent in 1998 to 25.6 per cent in 2004 (page 12), with the conventional bundle of an agent and the MLS, for which realtors charge a commission at around 6 per cent (page 2). The abstract says the authors do not find support for the hypothesis that listing on the MLS helps sellers obtain a significantly higher price, and that listing on the MLS shortens the time to sell. The estimated premium for selling by the owner is about 3 per cent after controls for the house and the neighbourhood (3.2 per cent, page 15), and the text also says the price premium for listing on the website is 3.1 per cent (page 15) and discusses selection of sellers into the website (pages 21 to 22), including a seller-fixed-effects check on 216 sellers who used both platforms. What the agent sells, on this evidence, is speed and a higher chance of selling, not a better price. The published version, in the American Economic Review 99(5), 1878 to 1898 (2009), is reported to add that patient sellers choose the website and patient buyers use the MLS, which I read only in an abstract and did not check.

CAUTIONS

The estimates rest on the assumption that, once the controls are included, the choice of platform is as good as random, which the authors discuss but do not claim to have established. The price is the sale price, and the commission is not netted off, so a premium for selling by the owner is on top of the commission saved. One city and a period in which the platform was new. The paper treats the platforms as a two-sided network with increasing returns, and the welfare discussion is the part to read if the question is how the market is structured.

SOURCE

Hendel, I., Nevo, A. and Ortalo-Magné, F. (2007), NBER Working Paper 13360, abstract, page 2 and Table 1 (page 29); the price results are on pages 14 to 15. Published in the American Economic Review 99(5), 2009, 1878 to 1898.

A CASE COULD SUPPLY

For an asset the guest has sold: how long the sale took, whether an adviser or broker ran the process, what it was paid, and what the seller would have done without one.
text: Selling a House without an Agent 4 The comparison: Madison, Wisconsin, 1998 to 2004: 3,138 homes listed by the owner on a website, 12,468 listed with an agent Success: 86.0 per cent of agent listings sold through the agent, 68.6 per cent of owner listings sold by the owner; 22.2 per cent of owner listings ended with an agent Price: no support for a higher price through the agent; the premium for selling by the owner was about 3 per cent after controls Time: listing with an agent shortens the time to sell The reading: the agent sells speed and a better chance of a sale, not a better price Hendel, Nevo and Ortalo-Magné (2007), NBER Working Paper 13360, Table 1 (page 29) and pages 14 to 15; abstract. Published in the American Economic Review 99(5), 2009.

title: Agents' Fees after the 2024 Settlement
notes:
THE FIGURE

Buchak, Matvos, Piskorski and Seru, NAR Settlement, House Prices, and Consumer Welfare, NBER Working Paper 32855, August 2024, revised October 2025, printed pages 16 to 17 and Figure 1 (page 31; PDF page less one). The authors calibrate a dynamic structural search model of the US housing market in which the seller pays all agent fees and reduce the combined fee from the 6 per cent baseline. House prices rise by 1.25 per cent at a 5 per cent fee, 2.5 per cent at 4, 4 per cent at 3 and 9 per cent at 0. Consumer welfare rises by 1.75, 3.25, 4 and 9.5 per cent. The text states only these points, and the chart draws only these.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The institution: in the United States the seller pays both agents, a typical 5 to 6 per cent of the sale price and among the highest in the world, more than double the average outside the United States on one estimate they cite (page 2 and footnote 1). The settlement of litigation by the National Association of Realtors took effect on 17 August 2024 and removed the requirement to post the buyer agent's offered commission on the MLS (Buchak et al., page 2; the ban on posting the buyer agent's offer on the MLS is described by Grochulski and Wang, page 2). The finding that runs against intuition: lower fees raise house prices, because lower future transaction costs raise the value of housing as a durable asset (abstract). Most of the welfare gain accrues to current owners, with limited benefits for prospective buyers, and higher prices may crowd out financially constrained households (abstract). The alternative reading is Grochulski and Wang, Real Estate Commissions and Homebuying, Richmond Fed Working Paper 24-01R, December 2025: in their model the buyer agent's commission of 3 per cent, which 96.5 per cent of 2.58 million Houston listings from 1997 to 2019 offered exactly, deviates from cost, generating excess profit and too much searching, and a cost-based system could raise welfare by about USD 38.5 billion a year, mostly by reducing agents' rents (abstract and introduction).

CAUTIONS

Both are models calibrated to the US market, and neither measures what actually happened to prices and commissions after August 2024. The two papers also ask different questions: the first about the price level and who gains, the second about search efficiency and rents. Both are working papers. The settlement itself is a US event; the lesson for this week is what happens to the demand for an intermediary when the fee for it moves, and who captures the gain from a lower price of intermediation.

SOURCE

Buchak, G., Matvos, G., Piskorski, T. and Seru, A. (2025), NAR Settlement, House Prices, and Consumer Welfare, NBER Working Paper 32855, revised October 2025, abstract, pages 2, 16 to 17 and Figure 1. Grochulski, B. and Wang, Z. (2025), Real Estate Commissions and Homebuying, Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond Working Paper 24-01R, December 2025, abstract and pages 1 to 3.

A CASE COULD SUPPLY

Where the intermediary's fee was negotiated and where it was posted, and what happened to the fee and the volume when a competitor or a rule change arrived.
text: Agents' Fees after the 2024 Settlement 4 The institution: the seller pays both agents, typically 5 to 6 per cent of the price; the buyer agent's 3 per cent was posted on the MLS until August 2024 The prediction: a calibrated model says that cutting the combined fee from 6 to 4 per cent raises house prices by 2.5 per cent, because resale becomes cheaper Who gains: consumer welfare rises by 3.25 per cent, but most of it accrues to current owners Another account: Grochulski and Wang: a cost-based fee system would add about USD 38.5 billion a year, mostly by cutting agents' rents Buchak, Matvos, Piskorski and Seru (2025), NBER Working Paper 32855, pages 16 to 17 and Figure 1; Grochulski and Wang (2025), Richmond Fed Working Paper 24-01R. Model results, not outcomes after the settlement.

title: Investment Consultants as Gatekeepers
notes:
THE POINTS

Jenkinson, Jones and Martinez, Picking Winners? Investment Consultants' Recommendations of Fund Managers, September 2014 draft of the paper published in the Journal of Finance (I recall volume 71, 2016, which I did not check). I could read only the first eight pages of the draft, the abstract and introduction, so the numbers are those the authors give in the introduction. Printed page is PDF page less one.

The role: investment consultants advise institutional investors on asset allocation, benchmarks, active or passive management, manager selection and monitoring. An estimated USD 25 trillion of institutional assets worldwide was advised on by consultants as at June 2011, and 82 per cent of US public plan sponsors use them (page 1). Consultants are 'key gatekeepers' whose opinions decide whether a plan sponsor will even consider a fund (page 1). The influence: attracting or losing the recommendation of one third of the consultants changes the size of a product by about 10 per cent, or USD 0.8 billion, within a year (page 4). The performance: on a value-weighted basis there is no evidence that recommended products outperform; on an equally weighted basis they earn about 1 per cent less than others, a difference that is statistically significant in every specification; the underperformance is explained by the scale of the recommended funds, and controlling for size there is still no evidence that the recommendations produced alpha (pages 5 to 6). What the consultants may add: hand-holding and trust (the 'money doctor' of Gennaioli and others), a shield that lets a sponsor defend its decisions, and a misunderstanding of what recommendations are worth, given that consultants do not disclose their own past recommendations (page 6).

THE LIMIT

The sample is US actively managed equity, from 1999 to 2011, using Greenwich Associates survey data on recommendations. The authors say that this may be a more efficient asset class than others, and that elsewhere consultants may be more prescient (page 6). Nothing here is evidence about infrastructure funds, where the investors' own capacity to choose is weaker and the consultants' role in the market for funds is large.

THE LINK TO THE MODELS

This slide is evidence for the second model of the focus part: flows follow recommendations and not performance, and recommended funds do not outperform, which is what Berk and Green predict when investors compete for the manager's output. It is also about assurance, the third model: a consultant sells an approval that others rely on, and, as the authors point out, does not disclose its own record.

SOURCE

Jenkinson, T., Jones, H. and Martinez, J. V. (2014), Picking Winners? Investment Consultants' Recommendations of Fund Managers, September 2014 draft, pages 1 to 6.

A CASE COULD SUPPLY

How the principal chooses managers: whether a consultant recommends them, what it is paid, and whether the principal has ever checked the record of its recommendations.
text: Investment Consultants as Gatekeepers 4 Their role: advise institutions on which managers to hire; about USD 25 trillion of assets was advised on in June 2011 Influence: winning the recommendation of one third of consultants brings about 10 per cent, USD 0.8 billion, within a year Performance: recommended funds earned about 1 per cent less than others, equally weighted; none outperformed once their size is allowed for What consultants may add: reassurance, and cover for a sponsor that has to defend its choice The limit: US active equity only; the authors say other asset classes may differ Jenkinson, Jones and Martinez (September 2014 draft), pages 1 to 6. Published in the Journal of Finance, which I recall as volume 71 (2016).

title: Private Credit and the AI Boom
notes:
THE TABLE

Aldasoro, Doerr and Rees, Financing the AI boom: from cash flows to debt, BIS Bulletin No 120, 7 January 2026. Printed page is PDF page less two. The table gives the Bulletin's own figures. Funds' assets under management grew from around USD 100 billion in 2010 to over USD 2.2 trillion (page 3, footnote 4, citing IMF 2024 and Avalos and others 2025). Outstanding direct loans to AI-related firms went from near zero to over USD 200 billion, and the share of private credit loans going to them from under 1 per cent to almost 8 per cent (page 4, Graph 3.A). Funds originated over USD 40 billion of loans to AI-related companies in 2025, against about USD 3 billion in 2010, and the share of AI-related direct loans in originations rose from close to 0 to about 4 per cent (page 4, footnote 5). The spreads on private credit loans to AI firms are close to those on loans to non-AI firms, and the difference stays insignificant after accounting for loan size, maturity, security and borrower characteristics (page 5, Graph 3.C and footnote 6). 'AI firms' here are firms in the PitchBook verticals Artificial Intelligence, Big Data and Cloud Tech, so the data are about borrowers in the AI industry and not about data-centre projects as such.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The Bulletin says that debt is replacing operating cash flow as the main source of finance for the five firms that drive the boom (Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle), that risks in construction, power availability and tenant concentration put some financing outside the scope of traditional bank and bond finance, and that private credit, whose bespoke covenants, speed and flexibility on renegotiation suit large asset-heavy projects, is the fastest-growing source (page 3). It describes private credit as non-bank credit extended by funds that negotiate directly with the borrower and hold the loan until maturity (page 3), and the funds as mostly closed-end vehicles that lock capital in for around four to eight years (footnote 4). It also warns that some structures may mask leverage by moving it off the balance sheet, that 'leverage does not disappear by being out of sight', and that circular financing within the AI ecosystem is a source of concern (page 4). The disconnect it points to is between loan spreads that treat an AI borrower as an average one and equity valuations that imply outsized future returns: either lenders underestimate risk or equity investors overestimate cash flow (page 5).

THE WEEK'S ANGLE

This is the week's aspect of the course thread on data centres. The question is not how big the boom is, which Weeks 1 and 2 covered, nor how a single deal is structured, which Week 4 did with Hyperion. It is who stands between the hyperscaler and the capital: a fund that originates and holds, in the way slide 4 contrasts with originate-to-distribute banks. A fund that holds to maturity has no secondary market to offload risk, which links the slide to the first model of the focus part, immediacy.

CAUTIONS

A Bulletin of 8 pages with graphs from PitchBook data. The endpoint figures are as the text gives them; the series themselves are not reproduced here because only the endpoints are stated in the text. A widely quoted figure for the share of private credit going to AI firms is the Bulletin's and depends on the PitchBook classification. I did not retrieve who arranged or bought the Hyperion financing, and the slide makes no claim about it.

SOURCE

Aldasoro, I., Doerr, S. and Rees, D. (2026), Financing the AI boom: from cash flows to debt, BIS Bulletin No 120, 7 January 2026, pages 3 to 5 and footnotes 4 to 6.

A CASE COULD SUPPLY

Who originated and who holds the data-centre or infrastructure loans the principal knows of, on what terms, and what happens if the holder wants to sell.
text: Private Credit and the AI Boom 4 Funds lend directly and hold the loan to maturity. The Bulletin warns that some structures move leverage off the balance sheet, and notes circular financing within the AI ecosystem (page 4). Aldasoro, Doerr and Rees (2026), BIS Bulletin No 120, 7 January 2026, pages 3 to 5. 'AI firms' are PitchBook's Artificial Intelligence, Big Data and Cloud Tech verticals. title: Three Models of What Intermediaries Sell
notes:
WHAT THE SLIDE SAYS

Three things an intermediary can sell, each with a model that I read in the original and a page that runs it. Immediacy: a dealer who is found shortens a search. Skill: a manager has a talent that investors cannot see, and that competition leaves with the manager. Assurance: a certifier gives an approval that others rely on, and liability is what makes it worth having. The test at the foot of the slide is the question to carry into the case: for any intermediary, which of the three does it sell, what is it paid, and who bears the loss if it fails.

HOW THEY FIT

They are three answers to the question that frames the week: what are the fees for. The four frictions of the earlier deck (search, information asymmetry, verification cost, agency) collapse into three because verification and information asymmetry are both met by an approval someone else will stand behind. The first hour has already given evidence for each: the fee stack and the placing of loans (slides 3 and 4), the sale of houses and the consultants' record (slides 6 to 8) and arranger prestige (slide 5). The three pages should be run in the order of the slides. They differ in what they hold fixed. The dealer model fixes the investors and varies how easily they meet. The fund model fixes the investors' competition and varies skill. The certification model fixes the firms and varies the liability.

WHY THESE THREE

I chose them because each has a source that I could read in full or whose key results I could derive and check, each has a closed form that runs in a browser, and each is a different kind of claim: a price, a rent and a quality. Alternatives I considered and could not retrieve: Bolton, Freixas and Shapiro (2012) on rating agencies, which would have put competition between agencies and the choice of a rating at the centre; Lizzeri (1999) on certification and information disclosure; and Gârleanu and Pedersen (2018) on efficiently inefficient markets for assets and asset management, a model that combines the first two models of this week. Franzoni (1999), which is not published in a journal that I could find, stands in for the certification literature.

RECENT SOURCES

For each model the slide sets alongside a recent source: for the dealer, nothing on infrastructure that I could verify, which is itself a finding about how thin the evidence on secondary markets for unlisted assets is; for the fund, Berk and van Binsbergen (2012) on the dollars mutual fund managers add; for the certifier, the evidence on arranger certification in project finance (slide 5) and the consultants' record (slide 8).

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

Whichever case is chosen, ask the guest which of the three each intermediary in the transaction sold, what each was paid, and what would have happened without it. A case in which an intermediary can be identified that sold none of the three is a case of a toll.
text: Three Models of What Intermediaries Sell 4 Immediacy: Duffie, Gârleanu and Pedersen (2005): a dealer is paid for shortening a search Skill: Berk and Green (2004): a manager is paid for a talent that investors cannot see and that competition leaves with the manager Assurance: Franzoni (1999): a certifier is paid for an approval that others rely on, and liability keeps it honest The test: for any intermediary, say which of the three it sells, what it is paid, and who bears the loss if it fails

title: Duffie et al. (2005): Search and the Dealer
notes:
THE MODEL

Duffie, Gârleanu and Pedersen (2005), Over-the-Counter Markets, Econometrica 73(6), 1815 to 1847; I read NBER Working Paper 10816 (November 2004), pages 5 to 17, where printed page is PDF page less two. Investors hold at most one unit of an asset that pays 1 a year and are of a high or a low type, the low types bearing a holding cost. They meet at random, at a rate λ with other investors and ρ with dealers. A dealer takes either side and lays the position off immediately in an inter-dealer market, so holds no inventory. Prices come from bargaining: investors with each other (seller's power q), investors with dealers (dealer's power z). The steady-state masses of the four types solve a quadratic (equations 3 to 6) and the prices are in closed form (Theorem 2, equations 11 to 13, page 13): each price is 1/r, the present value of the income, less a discount for waiting.

THE FIGURE

The ask, the bid and the price between investors against the number of times a year an investor finds a dealer, at the generic settings of the page (r = 5 per cent, holding cost half the income, switch intensities 2 and 1, 40 per cent of investors own the asset, investors meet each other once a year, bargaining power 50 per cent each). With no dealer the price between investors is 16.79 against 20 without frictions, a discount of 16.0 per cent, and an owner waits 16.1 months. With a dealer found twice a year the ask is 17.60, the bid 17.54, the price between investors 17.54, the discount 12.3 per cent and the wait 4.5 months. With dealers found twenty times a year the discount is 3.9 per cent. The ask and the bid are nearly on top of each other on the chart, which is the point of the next slide.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

A low-type owner wants to sell and a high-type non-owner wants to buy, but they must find each other. The dealer is a faster route and charges for it. The model is the simplest in which an intermediary earns a spread that depends on how hard the search is. The paper's comparative statics (pages 13 to 14): prices fall with the dealer's bargaining power and rise with the ease of finding a dealer or another investor; the bid-ask spread rises with the dealer's power, falls with λ, and falls with ρ unless the dealer has all the power.

CAUTIONS

Linear utility, one unit or none, no price impact and no information problem. The page covers Condition 1 only (the paper's natural case, in which there are fewer owners than high types). Dealers have no inventory cost, which is why the spread is small. The paper's later sections add risk aversion and endogenous search. I verified the closed forms against the value-function system of equation A.5 (agreement to 1e-12) and against the stationary distribution of the four-state chain.

SOURCE

Duffie, D., Gârleanu, N. and Pedersen, L. H. (2005), Over-the-Counter Markets, Econometrica 73(6), 1815 to 1847; NBER Working Paper 10816, pages 5 to 17.

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

How long a stake in the principal's assets takes to sell, how many buyers there would be, whether a dealer or adviser would take the other side, and at what discount to the value of the income. The nearest observable is the price of a secondary transaction against the carrying value.
text: Duffie et al. (2005): Search and the Dealer 4 Investors: high or low type, owning or not; a low-type owner wants to sell and a high-type non-owner wants to buy Search: they meet at random, and a dealer can be found too, who takes either side and holds no inventory Prices: each is the value of the income less a discount for waiting At the generic settings: with no dealer the discount is 16.0 per cent and the wait 16 months; with a dealer found twice a year, 12.3 per cent and 4.5 months Duffie, Gârleanu and Pedersen (2005), NBER Working Paper 10816, pages 5 to 13; Theorem 2, equations 11 to 13. Generic settings of the interactive page.

title: The Cost of Immediacy
notes:
THE FIGURE

The bid-ask spread as a share of the mid price against the number of times a year an investor finds a dealer, for four levels of the dealer's bargaining power, at the generic settings of the page. For a dealer with 20 per cent of the power the spread falls from 0.17 per cent with no dealer contacts to 0.03 per cent at 20 contacts a year; for 50 per cent the figures are 0.32 per cent at two contacts and 0.10 at 20; for a monopolist the spread rises, from 0.86 per cent at two contacts to 0.88 at twenty. The chart reproduces the two statements on pages 13 to 14 of the paper: the spread falls in ρ if z is below 1, and rises if z equals 1.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

First, the spread is small beside the discount. At the generic settings the dealer's spread is 0.32 per cent of the price while the illiquidity discount on a trade between investors is 12.3 per cent: most of the cost of illiquidity is the cost of waiting, which the dealer shortens, from 16 months with no dealer to 4.5 with one found twice a year, without removing it. Second, the spread falls as dealers become easier to find, because the investor's alternative to the dealer's quote, finding the next dealer, improves; that is competition by sequential search. Third, the dealer with all the power gains from being found more often. Fourth, an unlisted infrastructure stake is a different place. The preset for it has dealers found once every two years, few buyers (investors meeting each other 0.3 times a year) and a dealer with 70 per cent of the power: the wait is 16.6 months and the discount 15.8 per cent. These settings are a guess at an order of magnitude and not an estimate for any asset.

WHAT IT MEANS FOR AN ADVISER OR ARRANGER

An adviser or arranger is paid for shortening a search and for finding a counterparty. The model says its price falls when the client has other ways to find one, and rises with the intermediary's bargaining power. It does not say that the fee is fair. It says what to measure: the time saved, the alternatives open to the client, and the discount that remains.

CAUTIONS

The numbers are those of the generic page and are not calibrated. The page is for Condition 1 only. The expected wait, which is mine, is the inverse of the rate at which an owner trades, ρ plus twice λ times the mass of high-type non-owners.

SOURCE

Duffie, Gârleanu and Pedersen (2005), NBER Working Paper 10816, Theorem 2 and the discussion on pages 13 to 14. Interactive page: web/dealer-spread.html.

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

The gap between the price a seller would accept immediately and the price it could hope for by waiting, for an asset the principal has sold or tried to sell, and who was paid to close that gap.
text: The Cost of Immediacy 4 The spread falls with reach: from 0.32 per cent at two dealer contacts a year to 0.10 at twenty, for a dealer with half the power A monopolist: the spread rises with reach, from 0.86 to 0.88 per cent The discount is larger: a 12.3 per cent discount against a 0.32 per cent spread; the dealer shortens the wait but does not remove it An unlisted stake: dealers found every two years and few buyers: a wait of 17 months and a discount of 16 per cent Duffie, Gârleanu and Pedersen (2005), NBER Working Paper 10816, Theorem 2 and pages 13 to 14. Generic settings of the interactive page (dealer-spread.html); not calibrated to any asset.

title: Berk and Green (2004): Skill, Size and Rents
notes:
THE MODEL

Berk and Green (2004), Mutual Fund Flows and Performance in Rational Markets, Journal of Political Economy 112(6), 1269 to 1295, pages 1273 to 1277 (printed). A manager has an unknown ability a, so the gross excess return over a passive benchmark is R = a plus noise. Running a fund costs C(Q), convex in size Q. The manager charges a fixed fee f on assets. Investors supply capital without limit to any fund whose expected excess return after costs and fees is positive and withdraw from any fund where it is negative, so in equilibrium the expected excess return is zero (equation 3), which gives f_t = C(Q_t)/Q_t plus f, where f_t is the investors' belief about the manager's skill (equation 4). I take C(Q) = kQ²/2, which the paper's general convex cost allows, so Q = 2(f_t minus f)/k.

THE FIGURE

Fund size against the skill investors believe a manager has, at the generic settings of the page (average new fund believed to add 3 per cent a year, a fee of 1 per cent, a cost of size k of 0.4 percentage points per billion dollars). A new fund believed to be of average skill grows to 10.0 billion dollars. The fee income is 100 million dollars a year and the cost of managing the fund 200 million, which together equal the skill times the size, 300 million: the investors keep nothing above the benchmark. The second line is the size under the fee that maximises the manager's income, which is half the perceived skill; there the size is 7.5 billion and the income 112 million. This is the paper's result (equations 9 and 10, pages 1276 to 1277) that a fee that changes with perceived skill, or a fixed fee with part of the fund indexed, yields the efficient size, and I verified the half numerically.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The model reconciles three facts that the literature had found hard to reconcile: investors chase past performance, past performance does not persist, and active managers do not on average beat the benchmark for investors. In the model all three are the outcome of rational behaviour. The skill is real and it earns a rent, but the rent goes to the manager and to the cost of running a larger fund, not to investors.

CAUTIONS

Partial equilibrium, with a benchmark no one can move and a cost that depends on size alone. It assumes that capital can be moved at no cost and without limit, which is not true of a closed-end infrastructure or private credit fund that locks capital in for ten years or four to eight years. The quadratic cost is mine. The model says nothing about whether any particular fee is earned.

SOURCE

Berk, J. B. and Green, R. C. (2004), Journal of Political Economy 112(6), 1269 to 1295, equations 1 to 10, pages 1273 to 1277.

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

The size of the funds the principal chooses to invest in, how it learns about a manager's skill, whether it adds to a manager that has done well, and whether it has ever been unable to put more money to work with a manager because of capacity.
text: Berk and Green (2004): Skill, Size and Rents 4 Managers: differ in skill, which no one observes; everyone learns it from returns Investors: put money in until the expected excess return after costs and fees is zero Size: a fund believed to add 3 per cent a year, with a fee of 1 per cent and a cost of size of 0.4 points a billion, grows to 10 billion dollars The rent: the manager collects 100 million dollars a year in fees and managing the fund costs 200 million; investors earn nothing above the benchmark Berk and Green (2004), Journal of Political Economy 112(6), equations 3, 4, 9 and 10, pages 1275 to 1277. Quadratic cost and generic settings are mine (fund-rents.html).

title: Returns and Flows in a Population of Funds
notes:
THE FIGURE

The average gross and net excess return, by year of the fund's life, of 600 simulated funds that start together with skill drawn from the prior (mean 3 per cent, standard deviation 2 points) and noise of 6 per cent a year, at the generic settings of the page and the page's default random seed; a fund closes when investors would no longer break even. The shaded band is two standard errors around zero. The gross return of the survivors averages 3.3 per cent. The net return to investors averages 0.08 per cent over 8288 fund-years, inside the band in nearly every year, and the correlation of a fund's net return with the next year's averages 0.01. Pressing the button on the page draws another set of funds, and the result is the same in kind: this is not an accident of the draw, which the checks confirm on populations of 4,000 funds over five seeds.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The model predicts that expected net returns are zero for every fund at every date given what is known (equation 3), so there is no persistence, and flows respond to performance because performance changes beliefs about skill (Proposition 1, pages 1275 to 1276). The slide's last line is the empirical counterpart. Berk and van Binsbergen (2012), NBER Working Paper 18184, measure skill as the dollar value a fund adds, the gross excess return over its benchmark times the assets managed, and find that the average mutual fund manager adds about USD 2 million a year, that skill persists for as far as ten years, that investors recognise it and reward it with more capital, and that higher-skilled managers are paid more (abstract). The published version is in the Journal of Financial Economics, which I recall as volume 118 (2015) and did not check. The point for this week is that a manager can be skilled and its investors can still earn nothing extra, because the skill is captured by the manager.

CAUTIONS

US mutual funds, not infrastructure. A simulation of a model, not data. The result that net returns have zero expected value is an outcome of the assumption of free capital, as slide 13 says. For private funds the evidence is thinner and more mixed: I did not retrieve a verified study of the persistence of infrastructure fund returns, and the slide does not claim one.

SOURCE

Berk and Green (2004), Proposition 1 and equations 3 to 7, pages 1275 to 1276. Berk, J. B. and van Binsbergen, J. H. (2012), Measuring Managerial Skill in the Mutual Fund Industry, NBER Working Paper 18184, abstract. Interactive page: web/fund-rents.html.

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

Net returns of the funds the principal holds against their own benchmark over a decade, whether the best past performers went on to do better, and what the principal pays in fees as a share of the gross return.
text: Returns and Flows in a Population of Funds 4 Gross: the survivors earn about 3 per cent a year before costs and fees Net: investors earn 0.08 per cent on average, inside two standard errors of zero, and last year's net return does not predict this year's (correlation 0.01) The inference: the response of money to performance and the absence of persistence are what rational investors would produce The evidence on skill: Berk and van Binsbergen: US mutual fund managers add dollars, about USD 2 million a year on average, and the skill persists for up to ten years Berk and Green (2004), pages 1275 to 1276; Berk and van Binsbergen (2012), NBER Working Paper 18184, abstract. Simulation of 600 funds at the generic settings of fund-rents.html.

title: Flows after a Good Year
notes:
THE FIGURE

The money that flows into a fund after a return one standard deviation (6 per cent) above what was expected, by the year of the fund's life, at the generic settings: 3.0 billion dollars in year 1, 2.7 in year 2, 2.5 in year 3, 2.1 in year 5, 1.8 in year 8 and 1.4 in year 12. It is 2 times the weight on the latest return, κ/(g plus tκ), times the surprise, over k, from equations 5 and 6 of the paper (page 1275) with the quadratic cost. The weight is 0.100 in year 1 and 0.048 in year 12.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

Flows respond to performance, more for young funds than for old ones, because a young fund has a short record and one return moves beliefs about its skill more (page 1276). That is the 'flow-performance relationship' the model reproduces without any irrationality. The consultants' evidence on slide 8 is the institutional counterpart: the recommendation of one third of consultants moves a product by about 10 per cent in a year, while the recommended funds do not do better.

WHAT IT MEANS FOR PRIVATE FUNDS

The model is a statement about open-ended funds, in which capital can be added and removed. An infrastructure fund closes and locks capital in, so investors cannot move on a good year and cannot withdraw after a bad one; the response to performance comes at the next fund, when the manager raises a successor. That is a way to ask whether successor fund sizes track past performance, which the work on private funds can test and which I have not retrieved evidence for. The model also says that the capacity of a strategy limits what skill can earn: a strategy with a steep cost of size, such as lending to small projects, cannot absorb as much capital as one that scales.

CAUTIONS

The flow is a model output, not an estimate. The numbers depend on the prior and on the noise, which are generic.

SOURCE

Berk and Green (2004), Journal of Political Economy 112(6), equations 5 and 6 and the discussion on page 1276.

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

How quickly the principal adds to or withdraws from a manager after a good or a bad year, and whether the fund's size is limited by the opportunities available to it.
text: Flows after a Good Year 4 The weight on the latest return: falls with the length of the record, from 0.10 in year 1 to 0.05 in year 12 The inflow: after a one-standard-deviation surprise, 3.0 billion dollars in year 1 and 1.4 in year 12 Consultants: a recommendation from one third of them moves a fund by about 10 per cent in a year (slide 8) Private funds: lock capital in for years, so the response comes at the next fund, which the model does not describe Berk and Green (2004), equations 5 and 6, page 1275, with a quadratic cost; generic settings of fund-rents.html.

title: Franzoni (1999): Certification and Liability
notes:
THE MODEL

Franzoni (1999), Imperfect competition in certification markets, University of Bologna working paper, August 1999, pages 6 to 14 (printed page equals PDF page). Firms that want to engage in a regulated activity must produce a certificate of compliance. Compliance costs are uniform on [0, 1], the benefit of the activity is b (below 1), and a non-compliant firm that enters does social harm h (above b). N identical certifiers compete in quantities. A certifier pays s per unit of detection effort and, if a wrong certificate comes to light, which happens with probability α, is liable for a penalty P. It checks fully if αP exceeds s and not at all if it is below (equation 4 and Lemma 1). The demand for certificates is linear in the price (equation 7), so the market is a standard Cournot oligopoly. Proposition 3 gives the equilibrium; I derived the fee from the demand curve and checked it by brute force.

THE FIGURE

The price of a certificate as a share of the benefit, the quality of checking (the share of non-compliant applicants caught) and the share of firms certified, against the number of certifiers, at the generic settings of the page (benefit 0.6, harm 1.0, cost of checking 0.10, chance of discovery 0.5, penalty 0.6). With four certifiers the price is 0.20, 60 per cent of firms are certified and 67 per cent of non-compliant applicants are caught. With one certifier the price is 0.35, coverage 38 per cent and quality 42 per cent. With thirty, the price is 0.12, coverage 73 per cent and quality 81 per cent. The price tends to the cost of checking as the number grows (the paper says so on page 14), and coverage and quality tend to limits that fall short of the first best.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

A certifier cannot refuse a compliant firm, and it can detect a non-compliant one only by paying for the check. Firms know this, so when checking is likely, fewer non-compliant firms apply. Competition lowers the price and raises coverage, but it also encourages more non-compliant applicants, because the lower price lets more firms afford to comply and so weakens the certifier's incentive to check, so the detection rate has to rise to keep non-compliant firms indifferent (page 14). The paper's introduction concludes that more competition, or a cap on the price, may not be socially desirable.

CAUTIONS

One kind of firm, one kind of certifier, a fixed penalty and no reputation. A certifier that is also a lender, as an arranger is, has an interest in the outcome that the model does not capture. I could not read the paper's printed formula for the fee in the partial-coverage case and used my derivation, s plus (b minus s) over (N plus 1), which agrees with the paper's limits for large N. The case in which every firm is certified relies on the paper's assumption that the price is the highest at which demand is one.

SOURCE

Franzoni, L. A. (1999), Imperfect competition in certification markets, University of Bologna working paper, August 1999, pages 6 to 14, Lemma 1, equations 4 to 7, Proposition 3. Interactive page: web/certification.html.

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

How many certifiers there were in the principal's market for ratings, technical advice or arranging, what they charged, and what, if anything, a certifier lost when an approval proved wrong.
text: Franzoni (1999): Certification and Liability 4 Firms: need a certificate to enter; compliance costs are spread evenly, and only firms with costs below the benefit should enter Certifiers: compete on the number of certificates, and check hard only if the chance of discovery times the penalty exceeds the cost of checking Price: 0.20 with four certifiers against a cost of checking of 0.10, 0.12 with thirty Quality: the share of non-compliant applicants caught rises from 42 per cent with one certifier to 81 per cent with thirty Franzoni (1999), University of Bologna working paper, pages 6 to 14. Generic settings of certification.html; not calibrated to any market.

title: Liability and the Value of Certification
notes:
THE FIGURE

The value of the system, as a share of the first best (b²/2, the welfare if only firms with compliance cost below the benefit enter), against the penalty on the certifier when a wrong certificate comes to light, for one, four and thirty certifiers, at the generic settings. Welfare is the paper's (page 17): the net benefit of the activity less detection costs less the social harm of non-compliant firms that get through, with fees as transfers. At a penalty of 0.3 with four certifiers every firm applies, and the system is worth minus 16 per cent of the best outcome, which is less than nothing because the harm exceeds the benefit. At the generic penalty of 0.6 it is worth 52 per cent; at 6 it is worth 73 per cent, and no more however large the penalty becomes, since the fee still keeps out some compliant firms and detection costs money. With thirty certifiers at the generic penalty it is 53 per cent and with one it is 41.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

Liability is what disciplines the approval. With a low penalty the certificate says almost nothing, and most of the firms that apply are the ones it should have stopped. Raising the penalty improves the system quickly at first and then little (the paper's result for partial coverage, page 17; when every firm applies a higher penalty helps only if the cost of checking is not too high, equation 8, page 18). More competition among certifiers also improves it quickly at first and then flattens, from 41 per cent with one certifier to 52 with four and 53 with thirty. The paper's abstract and introduction summarise: the greatest possible liability is likely to be socially desirable, whereas regulation of the market, a price cap or more competition, may not be.

WHAT IT MEANS FOR ARRANGERS, RATING AGENCIES AND CONSULTANTS

The question for each is who bears the loss when its approval proves wrong, and how likely it is that anyone finds out. For a rating agency or an arranger the penalty is mostly reputational and the discovery probability is the probability that a default can be traced to the approval. For a consultant the evidence of slide 8 is that its recommendations are not disclosed, so the chance of discovery is low.

CAUTIONS

The page and the figure are of a stylised market. They show the direction and the order of magnitude of the effects, not the size of any real one. The numbers depend on generic settings.

SOURCE

Franzoni (1999), pages 6 to 8 (setup), 10 to 14 (equilibrium and comparative statics) and 17 to 18 (welfare and equation 8), and the abstract and introduction. Interactive page: web/certification.html.

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

The terms on which the principal's advisers and arrangers are liable if their work proves wrong, whether any has ever been held to account, and how the principal checks the work it is told to rely on.
text: Liability and the Value of Certification 4 Weak liability: at a penalty of 0.3 every firm applies and the system is worth minus 16 per cent of the best outcome, less than nothing The generic penalty: 0.6 gives 52 per cent A large penalty: a penalty of 6 gives 73 per cent and no more however large it becomes, because the fee keeps out some compliant firms Competition: 41 per cent with one certifier, 52 with four and 53 with thirty Franzoni (1999), welfare on pages 17 to 18 and equation 8. Generic settings of certification.html; not calibrated to any market.

title: Three Models Compared
notes:
THE TABLE

The three models side by side on the questions that matter for a case.

What the intermediary sells. Immediacy (Duffie, Gârleanu and Pedersen), a skill that investors cannot see (Berk and Green), an approval that others rely on (Franzoni). What disciplines it. For the dealer, the investor's alternative: waiting for the next dealer or the next investor. For the manager, competition among investors for the manager's output, which moves money to wherever expected net returns are positive. For the certifier, liability for a wrong approval. What the price reflects. Search frictions and bargaining power, in the first; skill and the cost of size, in the second; the concentration of certifiers and the liability, in the third. Who gets the rent. The dealer if it has most of the power; the manager, not the investor; the certifiers when they are few. How a case could test it. The time to sell a stake and the discount to value; the size, the fees and the net returns of the funds; the ratings, the liability terms and the defaults.

WHERE THEY ARE WEAK

None of the three is a model of infrastructure. The first needs many investors and no information problem. The second needs capital that can move at no cost. The third needs a single kind of firm and a fixed penalty. Each is nonetheless a test with a concrete prediction that an infrastructure case could confirm or contradict: that an asset with few buyers sells at a large discount whatever the dealer does; that a closed-end fund's fee is not a measure of the skill it sells; that an approval is worth what its giver stands to lose.

HOW THEY LINK TO THE REST OF THE COURSE

Week 1 has a fee-drag page (Andonov and others) that quantifies what a fund's fee and carry take from the gross return, and the second model says why investors might pay it. Week 4 has the Hyperion structure and the lenders' margin of safety, and the third model asks who stands behind the approvals that lenders rely on. Week 6 is about how unlisted assets are valued and reported, and the first model says why they sell at a discount that the reported values may not show. Week 7 is about disclosure and supervision, which are the third model's discovery probability.

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

The test at the foot of slide 10: for each intermediary in the case, which of the three it sold, what it was paid, and who bears the loss if it failed.

title: Case Study: Topic to Be Agreed (Justin Chiu, CK Asset Holdings)
notes:
AN OUTLINE ONLY

By design this is one slide naming the ground the case covers and leaving the discussion to the guest, Justin Chiu, Executive Director of CK Asset Holdings Limited in Hong Kong (his role as the speaker note records it). It states no facts about the case and makes no claim, so it cannot spoil what he says. No case is confirmed for Week 5: the topic is not agreed, and the title says so. He has agreed to serve on the Panel and has the case hour alone. The headings are neutral and could stand over any transaction.

WHAT I COULD NOT CONFIRM ABOUT HIS COMPANY

Helen's recollection is that his company controls a UK water company, sea ports around the world and the operator of the Panama ports. I could not confirm that these belong to CK Asset Holdings. A search shows CK Infrastructure Holdings (CKI), which owns UK Power Networks among other assets, described as controlled by CK Hutchison Holdings, with about 75.7 per cent, and CK Asset, which Victor Li describes as focused on real estate, as a separate company that sometimes co-invests with CKI. The ports, including the Panama terminals, are CK Hutchison's, and the proposed sale of its ports to a BlackRock and MSC consortium, announced in March 2025, was reported to have stalled, with a Panamanian court ruling against the concession in January and arbitration begun by the operator. I found nothing on the ownership of Northumbrian Water, Wales & West Utilities or a water company in the East of England. Please do not put any of this on a slide: the first question to Justin Chiu is which group entities he can speak for, and which of their transactions are public.

KINDS OF CASE THAT FIT THE THREE MODELS, WITHOUT CHOOSING ONE

Model 1 (immediacy and the dealer) is tested by any sale or purchase of a stake in an unlisted asset: the time it took, the number of buyers, whether a bank or adviser ran a process, the discount to the value of the income. A sale that failed or was withdrawn, such as the proposed sale of the ports, shows what happens to the price and the adviser's fee when buyers are few and political approval is needed. Model 2 (skill and rents) is tested by a principal that allocates capital to managers or operates its own platform: whether it hires managers, what it pays them, and whether it preferred to do the work itself. Model 3 (assurance) is tested by any financing in which a rating, a technical adviser or an arranger's name was relied on, and what each was paid and what was at stake for each.

KINDS OF EVIDENCE A GUEST COULD SUPPLY, IN ORDER OF HOW MUCH THEY ADD

A one-page account of a transaction the group did: the process, the advisers and their fees as a share of the price, the number of bidders and the time from launch to close. The terms on which the advisers were liable. The choice between a bank syndicate, a club of lenders and an institution that holds the debt, and why. The basis on which the group values what it holds, and how that compares with the prices at which comparable assets have traded. What is public, and what may be shown to students and later published in Cities: Global Perspectives, which needs clearance before drafting.

WHAT IS STILL OPEN

The case, the format of the session, the date and the entities. This slide does not propose a topic; the case suggestions for Justin Chiu, Humbert Pang and Steven Norris are written separately.

The same list as the Lecture Outline at the start of the deck, under a different title. There is no thank-you slide (Helen's rule, 2026-10-25): the summary is the last slide.

Run back through it one sentence per item. The sponsor of a EUR 200 million loan pays 1.75 per cent in fees before the first drawdown, and the arrangers keep very unequal shares, with those that stand behind the underwriting earning 3.4 per cent on the capital they finally lend and the managers 0.2. Arrangers with larger market shares place loans at lower spreads without higher fees, which suggests they sell capacity and certification. An agent in a house sale sells speed and a better chance of selling, not a higher price, and a model of the 2024 settlement says that lower fees raise house prices and mostly benefit current owners. Investment consultants move money and the funds they recommend do not do better. Private credit funds, which hold the loans they originate, have moved from nothing to about 8 per cent of their book in AI-related loans in a few years, at spreads that look like those on ordinary borrowers. The three models give three tests of an intermediary: what it sells, what disciplines it and who captures the rent, with the dealer's spread small beside the cost of waiting, the manager's skill captured by the manager and the certifier's value set by what it stands to lose. Then the case, where the guest tells us what the intermediaries in a real transaction were paid for.
